name: Hana Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing gets your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half four, because the cows don't care what day it is. I'm head stockperson at the Brennans' place, about 180 hectares, ninety milking cows, plus barley and a field of potatoes we sell to the chip shop chain in town. Milking, then feeding, then whatever's broken, and something is always broken. I love the cows, honestly, I can tell you which one's coming into heat by how she stands at the gate.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what keeps you there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The money wears me out. I've got a degree in agriculture and I earn less than my partner Jonah does driving the number 12 bus, and we still rent the little cottage off the farm lane. What keeps me there is the work itself, and old Mrs Brennan, who treats me like I'm the one who knows best, because on the herd I am. There aren't many farms left round here that still employ anyone, so it's not like I've got a queue of offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. Mr Brennan's son Declan keeps showing me videos of robot milkers and talking about apps for the herd, and I'd be the one at the union meeting saying the hype came to nothing. The cows still need someone who knows them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job stays roughly where it is, which is good and also not good. I'd still be on low pay with less than a month in the bank, still renting off my employer. The hype going away doesn't fix the fact that farm work is underpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, really. I'd keep going to the union branch on the first Tuesday of the month, keep pushing for the wage board rates to go up. And I'd probably ask Mrs Brennan again about a pay rise, because I asked last spring and she said after harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit flat, too, because relief isn't the same as things getting better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said relief isn't the same as better. What would better look like for you, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better is me earning enough that a broken fridge isn't a crisis. Last winter the fridge went and we ate out of a cool box on the doorstep for three weeks until payday. If AI turns out to be hype, I still have to save up for a fridge. That's the real story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the videos Declan shows you, would you ever try one of those tools if they stayed small and cheap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. I've never used any of the AI stuff, I don't even let my phone guess my words. I know a cow by looking at her, and I don't want a screen telling me something I can see.

S0.say: I'd tell people at work and at the union that the hype came to nothing and the cows still need someone who knows them. I'd say it with a bit of told-you-so.
S0.think: Honestly, it means my job stays where it is, which is good for the job but not for my life. I'd still be on low pay, renting off my employer, with less than a month saved.
S0.do: Keeps going to the monthly union branch meeting and keeps pushing for higher wage board rates. Asks Mrs Brennan again for the pay rise she was promised after harvest.
S0.feel: Relieved, but flat, because the old problems stay where they were.
S0.quote: If AI turns out to be hype, I still have to save up for a fridge. That's the real story.
S0.fieldNote: Her focus jumps straight from AI to pay; the technology is almost beside the point for her in this picture. The fridge story is vivid and shows how thin her margin is. She's firm that she won't touch AI tools even if they're cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Let's go to the next one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules, and fast. If machines are coming into milking parlours and fields, the workers should get a say in how, and the people who lose hours should get something back. I'd post that in the union group and I'd say it to anyone at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Declan gets his robot milker within a few years, and I go from head stockperson to the woman who cleans it and fetches the cows it rejects. The Brennans can't afford to pay me and buy a robot. Honestly, I think I'd be the first cost they cut, even if Mrs Brennan cried about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the union to push for a fair transition fund, money for workers moved off farms by machines. I'd stop buying anything that isn't food or rent, and I'd try to put fifty a week aside, though I don't know where it comes from. I wouldn't learn the robot, no. I'd rather fight for the job than train to babysit the thing that took it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Like when you hear a cow bellowing at night and you know before you get there that something's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather fight than learn the robot. If the farm offered to train you on it, paid, would that change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it should. I know it's stubborn. But I've seen what happens: you train on the thing, and two years later the company sells a version that doesn't need you either. I'd be paid to teach the machine my cows, and then it wouldn't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, apart from yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pavel, our tractor driver. He's fifty-eight, he came here from abroad twenty years ago, and driving is the bit that goes first with self-steering kit. He's got nowhere else to go, and he doesn't read well in English, so the retraining courses online would be useless to him.

S1.say: I'd say we need rules fast, and workers should get a say in how machines come onto farms. People who lose hours should get something back, and I'd say that at the union and at the market.
S1.think: I think Declan gets his robot milker within a few years and I end up cleaning it, or I get cut. The Brennans can't afford both my wage and the machine.
S1.do: Pushes her union for a fair transition fund for farm workers. Cuts spending to rent and food and tries to save fifty a week, while refusing to train on the robot.
S1.feel: A tightness in the chest, like knowing something's wrong in the barn before you see it.
S1.quote: I'd be paid to teach the machine my cows, and then it wouldn't need me.
S1.fieldNote: She knows she's being stubborn and says so, but she distrusts training as a trap. Her concern quickly spreads to Pavel, an older colleague with fewer options. Blame lands on companies and owners' economics, not on the Brennans as people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The next three are a different kind of picture. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when you let tech companies run the country. Nobody voted for it. I'd be at every protest going, and I'd be telling people online to demand a basic income, now, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished in farming within a couple of years, and I've got nothing to fall back on. I've got under a month of money. Jonah's bus would be self-driving too, so it's both of us, at the same time, in a town where there's no other work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, I'd still go to work, because what else? I'd sign up for every union action and I'd write to our representative every week. Once it arrives, we'd probably have to leave the cottage, because it comes with the job, and go to Jonah's mum's flat in the city. I'd sign on for whatever help there is the first week, no pride about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Scared in a way I don't really have words for, like the floor's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What's the first thing you'd notice changing on the farm, and when?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Declan would come in one morning with a brochure and Mrs Brennan wouldn't look at me. That's how I'd know. With two years, there's no time to save, no time to learn anything else even if I wanted to, so the short warning is basically no warning for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move to Jonah's mum's flat. What would you tell her when you arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we'll pay our way when we can, and she'd say don't be daft. I'd stand in her kitchen in the city with my good boots and nothing to wear them for. That's the bit that gets me, the boots.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when tech companies run the country and nobody voted for it. I'd be at the protests, telling people to demand a basic income now.
S2.think: I think I'm out of farming within two years with nothing to fall back on. Jonah's bus job would go at the same time, in a town where there's no other work.
S2.do: Keeps working while joining every union action and writing weekly to her representative. Once AGI arrives, moves with her partner into his mother's city flat and signs on for public help in the first week.
S2.feel: Sick and scared, like the floor has gone from under her.
S2.quote: I'd stand in her kitchen in the city with my good boots and nothing to wear them for.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year timeline leaves her no room at all: under a month's savings, a tied cottage and a partner whose job also goes. She'd give up the farm house and lean on family and the state without hesitation. The image of the boots carries her sense of loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same end point, a bit slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, but louder, because now there's time to do it properly. Five years is long enough to pass laws. I'd tell people online, if you sit on this for three years, it's on you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think five years gives the union time to win something, but it doesn't give me time to build savings on my pay. It probably means I'd be on the farm for three or four more years and then gone. It's a slower drop, but it's the same drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get elected as branch rep, which I've been avoiding because of the hours. I'd push for a deal in the wage agreement that farms using robots pay into a fund for the workers they replace. Jonah and I would also stop talking about moving to a bigger rental and stay in the cottage, because it's cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry more than scared. Angry gives me something to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change for you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes whether I go down fighting or just go down. With two years I'm a victim. With five I'm at least a nuisance. I'd rather be a nuisance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the robot earlier. With five years, would you look at anything new for yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something outside farming, like care work, which Jonah's sister does. Machines can lift people, I suppose, but I'd hope people want a person. I don't know if that's true though, I'm only guessing.

S3.say: I'd say the same but louder, because five years is long enough to pass laws. I'd tell people that sitting on it for three years is a choice.
S3.think: Five years gives the union time to win something, but it doesn't give me time to save on my pay. I'd get three or four more years on the farm and then the same drop.
S3.do: Stands for election as union branch rep and pushes for a fund paid by farms that use robots. Stays in the cheap cottage instead of moving, and starts to look at care work as a possible next job.
S3.feel: Angry more than scared, because anger gives her something to do.
S3.quote: With two years I'm a victim. With five I'm at least a nuisance.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time shifts her from fear to fighting, but not to retraining in farming itself. She reaches for care work tentatively and admits she's guessing about whether it's safe. The 'nuisance' line shows how she sees her own role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so no excuses. Ten years is enough to build a proper safety net and to make sure the land isn't all owned by whoever owns the robots. I'd be saying that at union meetings and to anyone who'll stand still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is long enough for me to have a different life before it lands. I'd be thirty-seven. I don't love that the dairy goes, but I'm not hanging off a cliff with this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the farm for now and do the branch rep job. Within the first couple of years I'd do a part-time course in social care at the college on Station Road, evenings, if the union could get the fees covered. Jonah and I would try to save something, even a little, every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. Sad for the cows, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be thirty-seven. What would you want your life to look like by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kids, maybe, which we've been putting off because of money. A job where my back still works. And honestly I'd want to still keep a couple of house cows somewhere, just for me, like my gran did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you were firm about not changing. Ten years and you'd do a care course. What's different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time, that's all. I don't like new things, I'll admit that, but I can get used to anything over ten years. What I can't do is change my whole life between one milking and the next.

S4.say: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse not to build a proper safety net. I'd also push to stop the land ending up owned by whoever owns the robots.
S4.think: Ten years is long enough for me to build a different life before it lands. I'd be thirty-seven and sad about the dairy, but I'm not hanging off a cliff.
S4.do: Stays on the farm and takes on the union branch rep role. Within two years starts a part-time evening course in social care, hoping the union covers fees, and saves a little each month with her partner.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to breathe, and sad for the cows.
S4.quote: What I can't do is change my whole life between one milking and the next.
S4.fieldNote: Time is the whole difference for her: resistant to change, but not to change she can absorb slowly. She mentions children she and her partner have delayed for money. The house-cow detail shows what she'd keep of farming whatever happens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question, because it hits me and Jonah at once and we've got nothing in the bank. What would help is money straight away for workers who lose their jobs, and a guarantee that the tied cottage doesn't get taken off you the same day the job does. People forget that when a farm worker loses the job, she loses the roof too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everybody talks about jobs, but I'd want someone to check how the cows are treated once nobody's there at night. That's not a joke, that's my job.

headlineQuote: People forget that when a farm worker loses the job, she loses the roof too.
portrait: Hana Okafor is a 27-year-old head stockperson on a small dairy and arable farm, with a degree in agriculture, low pay, under a month's savings and a cottage that comes with the job. She's a union member who blames tech companies and farm economics, not her employers, and she refuses to use AI tools. If AI is hype she shrugs and goes back to fighting for pay; steady change makes her anxious and she'd rather fight than train on the robot. Fast AGI leaves her panicked, with her partner's bus job going too and a move to his mother's flat. With five or ten years she shifts to union organising and, slowly, to a care course.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and her partner would lose their jobs at once with almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: Immediate money for workers who lose their jobs, and protection so farm workers don't lose their tied home the same day they lose the job.
